# How to Start Using AI That Actually Does Things for You

> **In short:** Today's major AI assistants can take real actions in your apps — sending email, scheduling meetings, sorting files — instead of only answering questions. You can start in about ten minutes by connecting one app at a time and keeping approval turned on.

A few years ago, asking an AI a question felt like talking to a very fast encyclopedia. Now it feels more like talking to a coworker who can actually open a tab and get things done. That change happened quietly, and it's worth understanding because it changes how much time you can save.

## What changed

Modern AI assistants aren't limited to writing answers on a screen. They can use **tools** — a fancy way of saying they can open other apps, click buttons, and run tasks on your behalf. When an assistant has this ability, it's often called an **AI agent**: an AI that's allowed to take real steps in the world, not just describe them.

The shift matters because most of our day isn't answering questions — it's *doing* things: scheduling, sending, sorting, looking up. AI that takes action touches the *doing*, not just the *talking*.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- An account with a major AI assistant. **ChatGPT**, **Claude**, and **Gemini** are the most common starting points.
- A web browser (phone or laptop works).
- About 15 minutes for the first setup.
- Free tiers usually let you try at least a few action features. Paid plans unlock more connections and longer task runs. Check your assistant's pricing page for the current details.

Action features vary a lot between tools and update often. If your screen looks different from what's described below, that's normal — look for a "Settings," "Connectors," or "Integrations" label and you'll be in the right area.

## Step 1 — Pick one task you'd like to hand off

Before touching any settings, decide what you actually want help with. A useful first task has three qualities: it's repetitive, it's safe to try (low stakes if something goes wrong), and it touches an app you already use.

A few examples that work well for a first try:

- *"Find a free 30-minute slot with [name] this week and draft an invite."*
- *"Read the three PDFs in my Downloads folder and write a one-page summary."*
- *"Sort my recent photos into folders by month."*

You'll know it worked when you can describe the task in one sentence and you wouldn't mind if the AI got it 80% right.

## Step 2 — Open your assistant's settings and find connections

Log in to your AI assistant on the web. Look for your profile icon or name (usually a top-corner circle with your initials), then a menu item called **Settings**, **Account**, or something similar.

Inside settings, scan for a section that mentions **Connections**, **Integrations**, **Apps**, or **Tools**. The exact wording changes often and differs between ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, but the idea is the same: this is where you let the AI see and act inside other services.

You'll know it worked when you see a list of available apps — Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Notion, Slack, GitHub, and similar services are common starting points.

## Step 3 — Connect one app only

Pick the single app that matches the task you chose in Step 1. If you chose email, connect Gmail. If you chose calendar, connect Google Calendar. Just one.

Click **Connect** (or **Add connection**). You'll be asked to sign in to that app and grant permission for the AI to read and write on your behalf. Read the permission list briefly — you should see the specific **scopes** (the kinds of access) the AI is requesting.

You'll know it worked when the app appears as "Connected" or shows a green checkmark in the list.

## Step 4 — Run your first task with "draft and confirm"

Go back to the chat. Describe the task you picked, including any details the AI will need — names, dates, tone, format.

A good first message looks like this:

> 💬 *Find a 30-minute slot with Sarah Liu this week, then draft an email asking if Thursday or Friday afternoon works for a 15-minute check-in. Keep the tone friendly and short. Show me the email before you send it.*

Two things to notice: the message names a specific person and time window (concrete beats vague), and it ends with *"show me before you send."* That phrase is your safety net — most assistants will prepare the action and wait for your approval before doing it.

You'll know it worked when the AI shows you a draft (an email, a calendar event, a file list) and asks "Want me to send this?" or "Ready to apply?" instead of just doing it.

## Step 5 — Review, approve, or correct

Read what the AI prepared. If it's right, confirm. If something is off — a wrong name, a too-casual tone, an extra recipient — tell the AI what to change. This back-and-forth is normal and is how the assistant learns your preferences over time.

Once you're comfortable, you can start adding more apps or letting the AI run small tasks without confirmation. Still avoid turning approval off for email or messages in the early days.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Connecting everything at once.** It's tempting, but starting with one app keeps surprises small. Add more only after the first one feels smooth.
- **Letting the AI send in your name too early.** Always review before the first send. Approval mode is your safety net — don't turn it off until you've seen enough drafts to trust the assistant.
- **Vague first prompts.** "Help with my email" is too soft. "Find the three emails from my manager this week and summarize them in five bullet points" is concrete enough for the AI to act on.
- **Forgetting that AI can be wrong.** Even with tools, the AI can misread names, dates, or tone. Treat its output like a draft from a new intern — useful, but worth a quick look before it goes out.

## What this means for you

- **If you're juggling a busy week**: connect your calendar and email first. The time saved on scheduling and follow-ups is usually the most obvious win, and you'll feel it within a day.
- **If you study or learn**: ask the AI to summarize long readings into notes, then ask it to generate three practice questions. That's two useful tasks from one tool.
- **If you run a small business or work as a freelancer**: connect the apps you use most (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Notion) one at a time. A weekly "summarize my week and draft a Monday plan" prompt can quietly replace an hour of admin work.
- **If you're worried about mistakes**: keep approval mode on. You stay in charge; the AI does the typing.

## Wrap-up

Action-taking AI isn't a single product — it's a quiet shift in what your assistant is allowed to do. Pick one task this week, connect one app, and try the "draft and confirm" pattern. The fastest way to learn what this shift means for you is to do one small thing with it today.
